subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY PROBLEM OF INSTITUTING CANADIAN SYSTEM

speechtext:
Hon. RAYMOND MORAND (East Essex) moved concurrence in the second and final report of the special committee on radio broadcasting.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving concurrence I should like to take a few moments to explain some of the features of the report. First of all, let me assure the house that it has been a real pleasure to work with this committee, largely due to the wholehearted cooperation and assistance given by the members of the committee to their chairman. In fact, they took practically all the work away from me and as a result I found my task easy.
The evidence, coming from all parts of Canada and from practically every walk of life was well prepared. Your committee weighed the evidence, bearing in mind both its source and its kind. In a very short time after we had begun our work it became evident that radio was a weapon which if used in a destructive way, could do a great deal of harm, or was an instrument which, if well used could help to build culture and civilization. The science of radio is but in its infancy. A decade ago it was only a toy, and gradually it has gone through the various stages from the time when we tuned in or dialed to find out how far in geographical space we could reach and what stations we could find, until to-day when it has become a real utility of entertainment and education. It has developed as an aid to education more in the past two or three years than previously. We speak of it as a help in education not only because it may be used to teach the youngsters, but because it is a projected arm of education which helps to finish and instruct adults in their homes. To-day radio finds its way to the homes of the most distant frontiersmen on the very edge of civilization. With those facts in mind your committee undoubtedly realized that their efforts would have to be of a serious character, and that they would have to keep the future definitely in mind.
To-day radio is an adjunct or auxiliary to religious teaching; it is being used by the various churches. Some of us may listen to what is going on in our neighbour's church, without being caught at it, and while things may be running smoothly in our own churches 
we find, through the radio, that our neighbour's church is prospering just as well. Radio is a great help to the teaching of disease prevention, and the promotion of health measures throughout the country. Through the broadcast of weather reports it is an aid to agriculture and is most useful in police work and many other types of education and utilities.
Your references were very definite. We were asked first to study the Aird report. In 1929 a commission was appointed by the then government. It travelled throughout Canada, the United States and Europe making a study of radio, its methods of application and control in those various countries. A report was made in 1929, which until this day had not been implemented. We were very fortunate in having the help of the three men who made the investigations and prepared the report. They gave us valuable information, which could not be put into the short space of a report. Their work, however, I am satisfied, helped the committee to arrive at the conclusions now before the house.
Your second instruction was to provide a technical scheme that would give to Canada the type of broadcasting to which it was entitled. In order to do that it was necessary for your committee to obtain the help of technical advisers, and in the help we secured we were most fortunate-and I speak both of the advisers who were definitely attached to the committee, and from the department. A scheme is presented in our report which we believe will quite definitely give to Canada that type of radio broadcasting to which she is entitled. I shall take a minute or two to read and to comment upon a few of the suggestions we have made.
First of all we believe a thorough survey of the entire field should be made before anything definite in respect to changes should be contemplated. Secondly, your committee recommends that consideration be given to the use of five 50 kilowatt stations, one in each of the following provinces, namely, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, and in the maritime provinces three 500 watt stations, one for each province, or one large 50 kilowatt station, as the commission may later decide. In Saskatchewan and Alberta we suggest two 5 kilowatt stations, in each province, synchronized on a common channel. Further, a 10 kilowatt station in northern Ontario and one in western Ontario, a 1 kilowatt station at Port Arthur-Fort William, a 500 watt station in Toronto, and a 1 kilowatt station at or near Ottawa, Montreal and Quebec.

Radio-Report of Committee
It might be of interest if in a short way I were to try to give, from a layman's standpoint, something of the business of broadcasting in its technical sense. Having had only six weeks' schooling in the matter I feel I am not very capable of going into the various technical points, but I shall explain it in the way it appeals to me. Dealing with the air, one would naturally believe that that is the one thing of which there is an unlimited amount. Hon. members may call it air, ether or space, whichever they wish. Strange however as it may seem, for purposes of radio broadcasting the air is of very limited quantity. The spectrum or the amount of space allocated or possible for broadcasting is, first of all, divided by international agreements or conventions into that used for commercial purposes, that used for ship-to-shore' work and that allocated to broadcasting. On the North American continent there are ninety-six channels, or we might call them highways in the air, and over those channels the human voice or music may be transmitted to be picked up by your radio receivers. By that I mean that if ninety-six stations of, say, 50 kilowatts, were placed on the North American continent there would be no further room for more stations. They would completely cover the allotted space of air, or ether, so far as radio broadcasting is concerned.
As we know, that space must be divided among the United States, Mexico, Cuba and Canada. By definite electric waves set at definite rates they are able to super-impose music or the voice and carry them through those channels, in much the same way that one goes over a highway in the country. Because of the large geographical area and the resulting difference in time it is possible to put stations upon the air w'ith lesser power, three or four on the same channel, providing that the power is not such that they interfere with one another. For instance, it is possible to put upon the same channel a station in California and another in the New England states, or one in the maritime provinces and another in Vancouver, provided the power is not so high that they interfere one with another. That accounts for the large number of stations now operating on the North American continent, most of which are on shared channels. Up to the present time we have been using for radio broadcasting a certain number of channels that were not in use in the United States. There was no definite written arrangement of any kind, but by a word of mouth agreement we were using certain channels. I propose to put on Hansard what channels we are using now and

In addition, these channels are ideal for the type of community stations so necessary in many parts of Canada.
In the new agreement, the channels for all our high power stations have been chosen from the best part of the broadcast band, namely the low frequency end. In addition, care was taken to see that both geographically and in so far as their relative positions in the spectrum were concerned, these channels were as far removed as possible from powerful United States stations.
The proposed technical scheme does not contemplate using at the present time all of the power that may be employed on these nine channels. In fact the number of clear channels available will provide for a population twice as great as that possessed by Canada to-day.
This agreement does not mean that Canada cannot again approach the United States for a further allotment of channels, should such action ever become necessaiy. In fact it definitely established a basis for the division of channels between Canada and the United States, should future radio conferences increase the number of frequencies allotted for broadcast purposes. I think it is only fair to say that in view of our desire to establish such a chain of stations in Canada, the willingness of the United States to clear these channels is a friendly act that should be taken cognizance of by this house.

In the scheme of broadcasting certain things have been taken into consideration. Ample coverage for each province has been provided for. Further, 100 watt stations which give a coverage in daylight of at least a twenty-

five mile radius are provided for, and with the amount of available shared channels we are quite capable of establishing at least 175 of these.
After establishing the technical scheme the task which your committee was confronted with was to investigate and report upon the most satisfactory agency for carrying out such a scheme. A number of very definite problems presented themselves. First of all we did not have adequate coverage; secondly, there was no trans-Canada or interprovincial broadcasting; third, there was no body or machinery to plan or control programs or advertising; fourth, there was always the possibility of a monopoly being established. On this phase I would cite the words of Mr. E. W. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, who was kind enough to appear before the committee. Mr. Garland asked him:
You do regard radio, Mr. Beatty, as a natural
monopoly?
The Witness: I do, yes. I do not mean to say by that, Mr. Garland, that it is the only way in which it could be effectively dealt with.
Further, the chairman asked Mr. Beatty:
I think the committee are properly advised that you think that a Canadian national system of some kind is necessary in Canada?
The Witness: Nationwide, yes.
A number of witnesses gave very similar advice to the committee. It is rather interesting to note that in the United States at present it is considered by those who are studying the subject that there is being established very rapidly a radio monopoly. Before the United States interstate commerce committee Senator Wheeler stated that fifty-three of the favoured stations were given more than fifty per cent of the picked channels, while the balance of more than six hundred stations were assigned to the remaining thirty-eight channels. Senator Dill indicated that twenty-five of the forty cleared channels carried the National Broadcasting Company's programs, and twelve were on the Columbia chain, leaving three cleared channels for independent stations.
These were some of the problems which confronted your committee. Another feature which had to be taken into consideration was advertising. As all who listen to United States programs know, advertising is one of the primary factors in radio broadcasts in that country. In England advertising is not permitted at all, and that condition exists in other European countries as well. But because of the fact that we are in such close apposition to the United States it was felt by your committee that advertising should be

Radio-Report of Committee
permitted to a limited extent, since if it were entirely prohibited in Canada those United States industries having branch factories in this country or selling goods in Canada would have an unfair advantage over Canadian industries. Consequently your committee has recommended that five per cent of the time be the maximum permitted for advertising. Nothing is said as to the quality of the advertising, that being left to the commission, because much was said as to direct and indirect advertising, though no two similar definitions were given to your committee in this regard by any of the witnesses appearing before it. Undoubtedly that is something that will have to be dealt with entirely by the commission.
There is another point which I think cannot entirely be lost sight of; it is that the air is as much a natural resource as our waterways, our water powers, our crown lands or any other part of the public domain. Perhaps it is more important to consider this as a natural resource, since the purpose for which it can be used is very limited. It is possible for us to give away some of our other natural resources and still have plenty left, but in this instance the use to which this natural resource can be put is circumscribed.
Another problem which faced this committee, with which I think most members were familiar in more ways than one, was the question of the finances available for this purpose. In considering all these points your committee deemed it their duty to devise as simple a machine as possible to deal with these problems, so that a commission of three is suggested, with definite powers. These include power to regulate and control all broadcasting in Canada, including programs and advertising; to own, build and operate transmitting or receiving stations in Canada; to acquire by lease, purchase, expropriation or otherwise, any or all existing broadcasting stations; to enter into operating agreements with privately owned stations; to originate .programs, and to secure outside programs by purchase or exchange, and to make the arrangements necessary for their transmission. I should like to direct attention to this matter in particular, because telegrams which we are receiving as well as reports appearing in the newspapers indicate that the opinion is held that if this report is adopted it will mean the elimination of all programs coming from foreign countries. We also recommend that the commission be given power to determine the number, location and power of all broadcasting stations required in Canada; to control the issuing or cancellation of licences to broadcasting stations; to cancel the allotments of
channels to any stations, or to make substitutions of channels; to prohibit the establishment of privately owned chains of stations in Canada.

They are simply given the power to prohibit in order that there may not be established, by the assembling of a number of small stations, a definite chain that would come in direct opposition with the. larger stations established under the commission. We further recommend that the commission be given power, subject to the approval of the parliament of Canada, to take over all broadcasting in Canada and be vested with all other powers necessary or incidental to the fulfilment of the objects of the commission.
We have made some definite recommendations. The first is that it be the first duty of the commission to establish trans-Canada chain broadcasting, through the securing of the necessary land lines. It may be of interest to hon. members to learn that there are in Canada three distinct trans-Canada telephone lines that may be used for this puipose. Each railway has one, and by arrangement among the telephone companies there is a third direct telephone line from the Atlantic to the Pacific that may be used for this purpose. Your committee recommend also that a nationally owned system of radio broadcasting be instituted and that all stations required for its proper organization be eventually acquired, these to be financed from the revenues accruing through the business of broadcasting, without expense to the taxpayers through the public treasury.

speechtext:
It was not my intention to make any remarks on the presentation of this report, but on second thought, as a member of the committee, perhaps I might offer one or two comments. They should be few, I think, because the report speaks for itself. Moreover, the chairman of the committee has made a very complete presentation of the objects and purposes of the report.
Before I proceed further, I should like to compliment the chairman of the committee upon the ability and courtesy with which he presided over the deliberations of that body, There was complete and constant good feeling; in fact, there was probably never at any time a real difference of opinion, which, perhaps, was due to the suave methods of the chairman. I want to compliment him also on the method of presentation of the report itself, for it relieves me of the necessity of making any technical explanations such as he has given.

Radio-Report of Committee
Generally speaking, I think it may be said that we have followed fairly closely, although not too closely, the recommendations of what is known as the Aird report. The important principle which is recognized in the report, and was recognized unanimously by the committee and by almost all of the witnesses who were heard, was this: that radio is in itself a natural monopoly. One member of the house said to me, in the early stages of the meetings that we held, that radio was a use of the air and therefore should be as free as the air. Now that sounds quite plausible, but when you consider the facts, it is utterly impossible to suppose that radio can be as free as the air itself, because, as the chairman has explained, there are only so many channels that can be used, so that the number and the use of those channels are limited. Therefore, as he has said, since it is in every sense a great natural resource, there should be some sort of control over it. It having been established to the satisfaction of everyone that radio is a natural monopoly, then it was a question of deciding whether it should be a publicly owned and controlled monopoly or one privately-owned and controlled. It is perhaps unnecessary for me to say that I should be opposed to the establishment of a privately owned monopoly of radio. We were opposed to private monopoly. We also recognized this -and it is what we were trying to avoid in the presentation of the report-that present conditions might so develop that outsiders might acquire control of radio broadcasting in this country, which is something very much to be avoided.
Speaking briefly, the main objects we hope to attain if legislation is introduced based on the report, are these. First of all, we wish to give complete coverage so that every listener-in, practically every resident in Canada, will have an opportunity of listening in to the best kind of programs. We also hope to provide a reasonable control of programs. We hope to promote national sentiment, to encourage Canadian art and music, to promote education, to lead to an interchange of programs between various countries, because it is easily possible, I am informed, under the system we propose to establish, to obtain the very finest programs from other parts of the world: from Britain, France, Germany, Italy and other countries as well as from the United States.
I wish for a moment to remove some misconceptions and to answer some of the arguments advanced in support of the objections that have been taken to. the nationalizing, if I may so describe it, of broadcasting. It is a fact that under this system it will be possible
for any listener-in, any owner of a radio, to sit down and tune in just as he pleases on any United States or other program, whether it be a jazz program or one consisting entirely of classical music or anything else-Amos 'n' Andy or anything else he may wish to enjoy. He is not shut off from listening to the programs to which he has been listening in the past. In fact, I would say there is nothing in this report, if it is carried out that will [DOT]prevent the listeners-in in Canada from enjoying absolutely all the privileges which they have to-day, unless they be modified by the fact that a necessary control of programs and advertising will be vested in the commission which is I hope to be established.
Another objection which was raised, and I think it was a very strong and a very fair one, was the fear that under this system of public ownership there would be some five or six or seven great broadcasting stations and that the smaller stations of 100 watts and under, operating in the smaller centres of population, would be abolished and could not ibe reestablished, so that the people in the smaller communities would be deprived of the privilege of listening to their own matters of local interest, whatever they might be, such as speeches, public addresses, report of hockey matches and things of that sort. There is provision made in this report that smaller stations may still be maintained, much as they are now, under private ownership, although their programs and the advertising remain under the control of the central commission.

I am well aware that some people feel that this radio commission will have ideas which will lead them to give to the people programs which they think the people ought to have, rather than what the listeners-in desire. I hope that that is not true. I hope that the national commission will certainly do something, indeed a great deal, to promote the things that I spoke of-national unity, if you like-promote the purposes of education and other very desirable things; but as I said before, the listener-in who does not desire to hear that sort of thing is under no compulsion to do so and may tune his own radio to whatever kind of program from Canada or the United States he chooses to listen to.

Finally we recommend, of course, that the control of radio broadcasting be placed under a commission, and that all the fees derived from licences be placed in the hands of that commission.

I am not sure, but I hope
so. Here was another objection. People wrere afraid that we would recommend a large capital investment in the establishment of these stations. That is not the case. Those who have read the report and have heard the chairman of the committee speak will know that we are recommending no capital expenditures to be made out of taxes, but that the whole of the expenses of the radio broadcasting commission be defrayed out of the receipts for licences, and perhaps from one or two other sources.
In passing I would say this, in the past, even with the old licence fee of one dollar the government saved out of the money thereby received over $1,000,000. I am not sure but that the old government had a hand in that as well as the present government; I do not know, but about 81,100,000 was saved out of those fees after paying for the work which the government did in connection with removing interference and giving services of that kind. Personally I think that that was not a fair thing to do. I think that the licence fees received from the listeners-in should have been expended in the interests of those listeners-in to give them a better service, eliminating interference and so forth.
My hon. friend from Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) asked whether this commission would be non-partisan. I said that I do not know whether it will be or not, but if the government are going to carry out all the other recommendations of this report, surely they will have no reasons for refusing to cany out what I think was the final one, that the commission should be of a non-partisan character.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, what the committee had in mind was something that will make, not for the detriment of the listeners-in of Canada, but for the benefit of all of them, in greater degree than they have ever enjoyed before.
Motion agreed to.

In view of the difference of opinion that seems to exists between some of the ministers of the Ontario government and the Minister of Labour with respect to the trans-Canada highway, I should like to have some information so we may get the matter cleared up and let the people of new Ontario know what they may expect. Answering a question of mine on May 3 with regard to the trans-Canada highway the Minister of Labour said:
I understand that a portion of it has been declared by the province of Ontario, moneys have been expended and the work is proceeding to completion.
I think that was a very fair position to take. Answering my friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) on May 9, the minister again indicated that so far as this government was concerned, they were prepared to go on with the trans-Canada highway. Is it still the intention of the government definitely to go on with this work through northern Ontario on a fifty-fifty basis with the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The basis upon which the trans-Canada highway will be constructed must of necessity be the subject matter of an agreement between ourselves and the provinces. I am confident there will be incorporated in the agreement with Ontario a provision that the building of the trans-Canada highway will be shared equally with respect to expense. The agreement is not in being, and I have not had the full benefit of the views of the provincial government on it, this proposed legislation not having been passed; but it is the desire of this government to proceed with the trans-Canada highway just as expeditiously as the stress and strain of these times, so far as finances are concerned, will permit. I do not think I can say anything further.

I bring this matter up because of the difference of opinion between this government and the government of Ontario. The minister has given a fair answer, but not a very definite one. At any rate it is quite evident that the federal government is willing to consider the contribution of money to the province of Ontario-I am speaking only of that province because I am more familiar with it-if the provincial authorities desire to go on with the work. I have brought this matter up several times already this session, and I am getting a little closer to the view of the minister, although, as I say, he has not expressed it definitely yet. On May 7 there appeared in the Kenora Miner and News, the official organ of the Conservative party in that section of new Ontario, a speech made by the Ontario Minister of Lands and Forests before the Kenora town council, the Keewatin town council, the Sioux Lookout town council and some of the representatives from unorganized districts. Very specifically he states his regrets that he is unable to go on with that work because of the fact that after a conference with the Prime Minister of Canada the federal government has refused to or cannot contribute any money towards it. That is why I am anxious for some frankness in the matter. I think the minister will admit that if he is willing to consider a contribution towards it by the federal government he ought not to have the Minister of Lands and Forests of Ontario misrepresent the position of this government. That gentleman said:
Last winter work had been arranged on the 'rans-Canada highway on a fifty-fifty basis with the Dominion government.
I am giving extracts from his speech, because it is very lengthy. He proceeded:
. . . but had since been discontinued and the dominion was not contributing any more.

That is a specific statement. The report continues:
^Stating that he felt bad about it, Mr. Finlayson went on to say that he had hoped to finish the trans-Canada to Fort William to give the big loop or at least to join up connections with the Dryden area, but unfortunately this could not be completed at this time, although he hoped to keep camps working on the roads under the new scheme.
That is, anyone without a home may go there and work for board and lodging and five dollars a month. Further, he said:
Last winter it cost approximately $100 per man per month to keep them working in the bush. Under the new scheme it -would cost about $50 a month to keep them at work in the same camps during the summer.
Again:
But they would not be able to go on with the work of the trans-Canada highway on the same scale.
I point out to the Minister of Labour what the Minister of Lands and Forests proposes to do for the unemployed in northern Ontario:
It was felt that the municipal councils should get to work and say "What cuts can be made?" I own councils, school boards and all municipal bodies should get busy and cut down on expenditures, and cut down on taxation. There would be little or no road construction, and they must plan to take care of their own needy. They can't load it on the governments. It is suggested that they go to the people with Bteady salaries and ask them to give so much to a central municipal employment fund. If the people of the town will raise this money the provincial and dominion governments would each add a like amount for immediate relief. "If you will do something of that kind, we will join with you in meeting the situation," stated Mr. Finlayson.
This is a new policy, Mr. Chairman. This bill provides what might be termed direct relief, or the "dole." We have been told by the minister that he is prepared to consider requests by any province for contributions from the federal government to carry on certain works. While this bill is before us we have the Minister of Lands and Forests going up into northern Ontario and telling the municipalities that they must take care of their own needy people, that they must not load them on the governments. He used the plural form. That is a strange situation after the way that some of us got pummelled around the political platforms less than a couple of years ago. But that is not the point. We have here a bill to provide relief by the dominion in cooperation with the provinces, and then we have the minister of one of the provincial governments telling the municipalities they must take care of their own needy. He said, "If you will get those

Unemployment-Agreements with Provinces
men who have steady work to contribute to a fund to assist the needy, the federal and provincial governments will augment that fund also." That is why I think we really should have some definite announcement from the minister.
Again I want to offer a suggestion. As everyone knows, we have been constructing highways since 1921 through the portion of northern Ontario which I have the honour to represent. When the provincial government changed in 1923, however, politics began to be played with the highway. Work was closed down, and they promised to reopen it and do so and so provided certain candidates were elected. We have managed to get on fairly well because we have had quite a number of elections. The people in my part of the country welcome an election, because that is about the only time we can get any work done. The more elections the more roads, so I go to my people and say to them, "Well, are you not glad? There is an election on we will get some more roads built. Let us get this election over with so that we can soon have another and get more roads."
At any rate, we have completed the highway from the Manitoba boundary to Kenora and it is being officially opened on July 1. There we have about 127 miles of road connecting Kenora with the province of Manitoba. There is a distance of forty-five miles from Kenora east through to a great farming district, where the farmers are hemmed in without connection with the main road. If we could construct a highway over that forty-five mile stretch, from Kenora to Vermilion Bay, we would provide an outlet for that great farming district, and if we continued that highway another sixteen miles east of Dyment we would get to Ignace. This would connect up the whole of new Ontario, with the . exception of Fort William and Port Arthur, with western Canada and also with the United States. Those sixteen miles of roadway could be constructed for about $35,000. I know something of that country; there is a little muskeg, but it is fairly level ground. The forty-five mile stretch from Kenora to Vermilion Bay would cost about $8,000 a mile, or a total of about $360,000. Would it not be better to spend that amount of about $395,000 in order to give that district connections with western Canada and with the United States, rather than to put men on direct relief? We are being asked to give the government the right to spend money at their discretion, and we have the minister standing in his place and saying that the government is willing to contribute towards the cost of
the completion of that highway. On the other hand we have the provincial minister of lands and forests saying in Kenora that the municipality must be responsible for their needy, but that if those who have steady jobs will contribute to a fund for the unemployed, the provincial and federal governments will contribute to the same fund.
Under these circumstances I think the minister, for his own protection, should indicate to the house what he is prepared to do, rather than have the provincial minister of lands and forests misrepresent the attitude of this government throughout northern Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I cannot subscribe to all the observations made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, who says that the idea that municipalities and private individuals should subscribe to a fund for the purpose of assisting those worthy people who are inneed is a new policy. That is not correct. I know the hon. member would not make an incorrect statement knowingly, but in the city of Ottawa, for instance, there are organizations' which subscribe money for this purpose, and the city also helps. In my own riding private individuals have done the same thing; in fact the workmen of one camp subscribe so much per month to augment the fund provided by the municipality, the province and the dominion in order to look after their fellow workmen who are in distress. This is no new policy; it is nothing new for the people who have something voluntarily to assist those who have nothing. I therefore have no complaint to make against the provincial minister of lands and forests when he urges voluntary subscriptions to augment the fund which is to care for the needy in any municipality; of course this is no new policy.
I do not know that I could make any observation with respect to the conduct of the business of the province of Ontario, either by way of commendation or criticism, but coming as I do from the eastern section of northern Ontario I must say that I have never heard of the things that have been described by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I do not say this because the province of Ontario happens to have a Conservative administration, because the same thing obtained, so far as my part of northern Ontario was concerned, when , the farmer government was in power; the work proceeded. I know personally officials in the northern development branch and other branches of the public service, who were officials away back in the days of the Ross government. They have never been disturbed, and to-day they are just as stout

Liberals as they were then. I cannot let the observations of the hon. gentleman in that regard pass without taking exception to them.
What observations are you referring to now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman said, if I heard him correctly, that no money was spent on roads unless there was an election, that the more elections there were the more money was spent. I may have misunderstood the hon. gentleman's words, but that has not been my experience. I hazard the opinion that no other representative of northern Ontario will make such sweeping statements in condemnation of the provincial government as have been made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. Of course I want to keep within the rules of debate in this house, but I am almost persuaded to use more forceful language in describing a statement of that character, because that situation certainly does not obtain in the part of northern Ontario which I know very well, and that includes the greater part of that area. I should be very much surprised indeed if it obtained in the hon. gentleman's riding.
With respect to the trans-Canada highway, the Minister of Lands and Forests, Mr. Fin-layson, in his remarks as quoted in the journal to which the hon. gentleman has referred, stated-I gathered that this was the substance of it-that the work would not be discontinued but that .the camps that are now built ind re-equipped to take care of single men .vho otherwise would probably have nowhere to go, would be available to them and that they would be given food and clothing and some subsistence money and would be required to work. I do not think that policy should be condemned at a time like this. However, I do not want to continue the argument further than to say that this government has not yet entered into any agreement with the province of Ontario with respect to the work, for the very obvious reason that we have no authority; and while the subject has been discussed in an informal way with the representatives of that province, no agreement as to what can or cannot be done with regard to the highway has been entered into. I am just as anxious as any hon. member coming .from that part of Canada to see that the gap between the eastern part of Ontario and the western part of Quebec on the one hand, and Manitoba on the other, is bridged by a highway, just so soon as it can be constructed. But again, representing as I do a very large riding in that part of northern Canada, I am not going to take the attitude

of urging at a time like this that the road be built and that the province should contribute moneys which they, in their judgment, say they are unable at the present time to advance, sufficient to have the road built with any great expedition. In my view, the building of the road will continue, not, perhaps, as rapidly as the hon. member would like, but as rapidly as the conditions that confront us will allow. I do not think the hon. gentleman can ask me to go further than that, and I can assure him that so far as I am concerned every effort will be made to continue the work on some plan or another to be agreed upon which will ensure its continuance at the least possible expense and with as great a degree of expedition as possible under present conditions.

The last remarks of the
minister were, I thought, rather favourable, but I notice that in the course of his address he had to stop a little while because he could not find words with which to express himself in relation to some of the things I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I have not as great a
facility of speech as the hon. gentleman.

Had I been in the chair I would have said to the minister, "Go to it," because I could not myself find words with which to condemn the practice of the provincial government in northern Ontario. I am glad that the Minister of Labour does not experience in his riding what I have been experiencing for the last twelve or fifteen years in my riding. However, we have lived through it.
I want to point out to the minister again that the government is contemplating spending money in northern Ontario in direct relief. Is it a fair statement that the government does intend to spend money in direct relief in northern Ontario? I have heard him say that over and over again.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: This government will not spend it directly, no; we have no contact with the municipalities. That is obvious. Undoubtedly, however, if a situation arises in northern Ontario necessitating the expenditure of money in direct relief, there is no doubt in my mind that a prompt submission will be made by the province to this government, and I am sure that this government will take the appropriate steps to relieve the situation.

Well, it is not a question of a situation that is going to arise; it has already arisen. They have laid off the men who have been working on these camps.

I do not know where he got the authority for that statement, but that is what he said, and he suggests that those who are in Steady employment should contribute to a fund to which the provincial and the federal governments would contribute a small sum to help it along.

speechtext: He did not say that that was a prerequisite to the provincial and dominion governments' subscribing-at any rate, not as reported in the press.

This newspaper, the Mines and News, would not misquote the Minister of Lands and Forests on a bet. This is what he said:
It was felt that municipal councils-
He did not say the council of Kenora.
-should get to work and say "What cuts can be made?" Town councils, school boards and all municipal bodies should get busy and cut down on expenditures, and cut down on taxation. There would be little or no road construction, and they must plan to take care of their own needy. They can't load it on the governments. It is suggested that they go to the people with steady salaries and ask them to give so much to a central municipal employment fund. If the people of the (town will raise this money the provincial and dominion governments would each add a like amount for immediate relief. "If you will do something of that kind, we will join with you in meeting the situation," stated Mr. Finlayson.
He is speaking there not only for the provincial government but for the federal government as well. I would point out to the minister that that town is composed chiefly of workingmen-railroad men, pulp and paper men, sawmill men, and flourmill men. The railway men are doing very little, because since this government came into power they have restricted trade, both imports and exports, to such an extent that there is nothing doing on the railways, with the result that the railway men are out of work, and any of them who have steady jobs have been sharing their work with the younger men who are less fortunate. They have therefore very little to contribute to any fund. The Minister of Lands and Forests is solely responsible for the Act that the pulp and paper mill in the town of Kenora is closed down. The Ontario government have an agreement with Mr. E. W. Backus, his heirs and assigns, whereby they have obtained certain concessions from the province of Ontario. I know something about it because I helped to get it; and they got
it under the condition that they would work the mill to full capacity ten months each year, employing one thousand men; otherwise the whole concern would revert to the crown. I am not unreasonable enough to say that we should force an industry to operate when it cannot sell its products, but that is the concern of the Ontario government, and if for some good reason the Ontario government released Mr. Backus from operating according to the agreement, then in all conscience the Ontario government is responsible for taking care of the thousand thus thrown out of work. But the way the Ontario government apparently intends to take care of them is by asking others who have steady jobs to contribute to a fund to which the Ontario government and the federal government will also contribute equally in order to keep these people happy and comfortable and prosperous up in northern Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
give me the date of the agreement with Mr. Backus?

I can give the hon. gentleman a copy of the agreement if he desires. There were two agreements, one dated September, 1920, and the other dated January, 1921, if I recollect aright-I will get the exact dates. These agreements provided for the operation of the plant for ten months in every year, during which time a thousand men were to be employed, and any evasion of the agreement rendered the whole contract null and void ipso facto. I repeat I am not unreasonable enough to suggest that there might not have been some good reason for the Ontario government releasing this concern from operating its plant, but I do say that when the Ontario government did that it should take care of the thousand men and see that they are employed in remunerative work.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

That is not in the agreement at all.

That reminds me that the present Ontario government in 1923 told the people throughout the province that Backus had got millions of dollars' worth of materials for a song and that it was going to make him immensely wealthy. But today that gentleman, as the Minister of Labour has just said, is bankrupt; and instead of the Minister of Lands and Forests in the Ontario government insisting on the implementing of

My point is that the provincial minister is not insistent upon this agreement being carried out, and he now tells the people of Kenora that the road work is not going to continue and that the people there must look out for their own needy and not shift the burden on to the provincial or the federal government. When the present federal government appealed to the electors, one of the planks of its platform was that a highway would be built through northern Ontario at the hands of the federal government. It is a federal obligation since the last election that a highway be built through that part of the country, if only to carry out in a measure some of the election promises of the present party in power.
Further, if the federal government are going to contribute direct relief for unemployment, they should see to it that this piece of highway, totalling sixty-one miles and connecting up the town of Ignace and the farming district of Kenora and Dryden with western Ontario and Manitoba, is built. It appears from what the
minister and the Prime Minister have said in the house that the policy of the government this year is to be what is commonly termed direct relief. Therefore the question of giving direct relief to the many thousands of people who unfortunately will be compelled to accept the same, is very important. In giving this relief to the individual, is the Department of Labour or the government laying down any policy, or is this entirely a question for the municipalities or the provinces to settle?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I can only repeat what
I said some weeks ago when the resolution upon which this legislation is founded was before the house. The policy that was agreed upon at the Dominion-provincial conference which was held in Ottawa on April 9, and which was in session something over a day, was this: it was agreed that the provinces and the municipalities could not longer afford to project works as had been the case during the past year and that this was also creating a heavy burden upon the dominion treasury. Every province -was in agreement that the difference between direct relief on a subsistence basis and the cost of works was very large; I do not think I need go into that in detail. The provinces and the municipalities, of course, are the only ones that are in touch with local situations, and how the direct relief will be applied must of necessity remain in almost complete measure with the municipalities and provinces concerned. Whether or not there will be anyone in an advisory capacity representing the federal government, has not yet been determined for the very reason that the agreements themselves have not so far been drawn up, and of course the situation differs in the different provinces. While we are not consensus ad idem on all features of the situation, yet just as soon as this legislation passes, I hope agreements will De entered into, satisfactory to the provinces and to the federal government, with a view

to ensuring that during this period of depression, which I hope will not last too long, we shall not have it said that people are starving and cold or have no home, no place to go. That is an unthinkable situation. To that end governmental forces in this dominion are going to direct their attention. I do not wish to be misunderstood, and ought to say that it is not the suggestion or the intention of this or, so far as I am aware, any other government to imperil the standards of living, wage scales or wage agreements in any shape or form. We must draw a distinct line between subsistent direct relief and wage rates and standards of living. I do not wish to suggest that we should hurry along with the bill, because I want to give all the information hon. members desire, but it is very desirable that this bill be passed, because the provinces are pressing. I can assure the committee that we are having a most difficult time, but can do nothing until the legislation goes through. I do not know what arrangements the other chamber may have made, but I believe there may be a short adjournment there, and it is very desirable that this legislation pass as soon as possible.

I should like to know if in the arrangements for unemployment relief in the coming year the government will follow the policy adopted last year of putting certain things which are really public works under the head of unemployment and farm relief?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The question of projecting works on tripartite agreements, namely among municipalities, provinces and the dominion, or on bilateral agreements between the provinces and the dominion, was discussed at great length with provincial representatves. There was unanimity of opinion that works of that character should not be projected, unless in very exceptional circumstances, the reason being, as frankly admitted by provincial representatives and recognized by this government, that it is extremely difficult for those interested in such works to raise the necessary money. There may be, likely are, places in Canada where money may be readily raised, but in such localities there is very little unemployment. For that reason alone, therefore, the projection of such works is not desirable. I assure the hon. member the decision is not to. carry on works as heretofore but to direct the main efforts of all concerned towards direct relief.

Unemployment-Agreements with Provinces

Those are the undertakings about which I have been speaking. What is the policy of the government for the coming year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I do not know that a policy has been set. I must say, however, I am in agreement with the hon. member that it is highly desirable that the public works estimates, in so far as it is humanly possible, should reflect the expenditures in that department. Why the work set out in the report of the director was done through the agency of the Department of Public Works, I am not well enough acquainted with that department to answer definitely. If my recollection serves me aright, when this matter was under discussion before the Minister of Public Works gave an answer. Occasion might arise where public works, for which provision was not made in the estimates, might be desirable in a locality in which unemployment existed, and where men
could be employed on useful public works for purposes of subsistence. I cannot say, however, that such an occasion will arise, and so far as I am aware the government has not considered the matter.

I should like to point out to the minister his remarks on April 28 of this year, as they appear in Hansard. I shall read my question and the minister's answer on that occasion:
Mr. Elliott: Perhaps I can make it simpler for the minister. He no doubt has before him the report of the director of unemployment relief. Again I protest against the system adopted last year by which the Minister of Labour, who is charged with the administration of unemployment relief, puts in his report these items, then when the report comes into the house and somebody asks about an item the answer is given by the Minister of Public Works. I refer particularly to the Haileybury breakwater. The answer is given:	I cannot tell where the demand
came from or what are the needs for that particular work, because it came in under unemployment relief.

I can only give the

Whether that would give rise to any accounting difficulties I do not know, but my view is if the Dominion government initiate and carry out any work under the provisions of this legislation, then that work should be described in the report of the director of unemployment relief as coming under this statute and not under the Public Works department. I do not know that I can go further than that.
If that is the proper course, then the wrong course was adopted last year, because a work of that kind was done by the Public Works department, I am advised.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I think so.

Perhaps my hon. friend can tell me why the matter has not received the consideration which he assured me two weeks ago it would receive before the bill was brought down. At that time he said:
Certainly before the legislation comes down I shall be in a position to do so.
Is there any reason why he is not able to implement that promise?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I can only answer the hon. member by saying that if any dominion public work is initiated under this legislation and carried out, then it will be so styled in any report; it will not appear as a public work as such, but as a work carried out under this legislation. But what substantial difference does it make, if the work is useful and desirable and in a locality where there are people who need employment? Are we not rather arguing on formalities and not striking at the root of things?

I submit that department is in a much better position to do those works than any other department of government. At any rate that is the department that did them last year, according to the statement made by the Minister of Public Works.

I want to ask just
one question and then make a very brief statement in regard to conditions in that section of the country which I have the honour to represent, and in regard to which I have some knowledge.
The question relates to a statement previously made by the minister with regard to highway work. Will this department be prepared to meet any province half way, where the province may find that it can employ married men with families in highway work, giving them a remuneration equal to *what they would receive under direct relief, in order to provide them with food and the actual necessities of life?
That is the question, and the statement I wish to make is based on what the minister said in regard to the advisability of getting this legislation through. I believe there is no part of Canada where the effects of prevailing conditions are felt more intensely than in that part of Canada along the transcontinental line in northern Ontario, where there are numerous small pulp mill and lumber towns which have been virtually abandoned. There are no municipal organizations; the
people are without churches and in many cases without schools, and there are no individuals better off than the others. They are virtually in a state of pauperism. In a very considerable section of that country we arranged last year for voluntary relief committees to administer general relief, and we secured assistance in the usual way from the provincial government. That assistance ended, however, on the last day of April. It was administered on a mere subsistence basis. There are many large families in that district at the present time who are absolutely in want, simply because for weeks past we have been discussing this and other legislation with regard to the question of relief.
I want to read one or two paragraphs from letters I have received in the past two or three days with regard to the conditions prevailing. I have this letter from the chairman of one of the committees:
There are people in this district who are actually starving. I am receiving pathetic appeals on every mail from parents, stating that their children are actually in want and without food. ... I got in touch with Mr. Morse early last week by telephone.
Mr. Morse is one of the members of the committee in one of the smaller localities.
I asked Mr. Morse to keep a close watch and advise me if any families were really starving. On Saturday Mr. Morse called me up and informed me that . . . one young girl had collapsed that day for want of nourishment and that ethers were on the verge of the same condition.
At the same time Mr. Morse also wrote me, because I asked these people to keep me. informed as to conditions. Mr. Morse said:
I may say that I went to Toronto last week in an effort to get a small interim grant to keep these people going, but was informed by Mr. Ellis that they could do nothing until the legislation was through in Ottawa.
Mr. Morse continues:
The two Tremblay families are starving. . . . There are many young children and a tragedy may occur there at any time. Nothing is being done and . . . they cannot hold out very long.
I have received many such representations. The situation is extremely acute, and while we take weeks to discuss the details, the methods and all sorts of questions, constitutional and otherwise, these people are actually starving to death because they cannot obtain relief.

There is one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I have received a communication from the unemployed, association of West Kildonan, which is a suburb of Winnipeg, and which is in my constituency. The secretary advises me that the standard of living has

been cut down, and that the rations provided are not adequate for the proper subsistence of the children. I understand also that the school teachers in that section have been supplying some milk in order to properly nourish the children.

I should like to ask the minister if this question has been contemplated in connection with any agreement which might be made with the provinces. The first question is this: Is there a standard of living that should be insisted upon, and in the second place, where does the responsibility rest?
There is one other matter that arises out of this situation. I have received a communication from the clerk of the municipality to the effect that 108 homes of unemployed people will be offered for tax sale this spring. It seems to me if we are to loan money to the municipalities for direct relief the unemployed ought to be protected to this extent: First, that the relief granted be sufficient, and second, that the unemployed should not lose their homes or their little market gardens because of their inability to pay taxes. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, and I would like to know if the government has any policy in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
It is obvious that the
matters to which the hon. member has referred come directly under the jurisdiction of the municipalities on the one hand and of the provinces on the other. It is utterly impossible for this government, without having contact with these details-and I do not use the word in the sense that they are not important-to have anything to do with these matters. I cannot conceive that the province of Manitoba, with the funds available for direct relief, would supply relief on which people cannot subsist.

I should like to ask a question of the minister in connection with the municipalities. On page 56 of the report of the director of unemployment relief there are
[Mr. J. H. Stitt.)
schedules of work approved in connection with many municipalities in British Columbia. I should like to ask the minister whether the municipalities will be allowed to complete the public works, such as roads and so on, that have been approved under these schedules. Many of these agreements were not given approval until December or January of this year, and I should like to know if these municipalities will be allowed to carry out those programs of work which have been approved.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
This debate has gone on
so long now that I assume hon. members have forgotten what was said when we began. I made it plain then, as will be seen in Hansard, what works would be proceeded with and what works would not. Under three headings a telegram was sent to each province, setting out the works that would be gone on with, or discontinued as the case might be. That was done by agreement with the provincial authorities, and I cannot add more to what I have already said on the matter.

This is very serious and a
definite statement should be forthcoming. I have to-day received a telegram from one of the municipalities, indicating the seriousness of the situation there. In that municipality there is still unexpended the sum of $43,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Is that Burnaby?

Yes. I had an interview with the minister's secretary and was informed that if these projects, to the extent of $43,000, had been contracted for and there might be a lawsuit if they were not gone on with, they would be proceeded with. But, I was told, if it were simply a matter of carrying on road work under the agreement, it would be stopped. I took the trouble to telegraph to that municipality, inquiring regarding this matter so that I might have definite information, and a few minutes ago I received a telegram to the effect that timber and other material for the necessary trench work had been contracted for and that the situation would be quite serious if the work were not gone on with. They have also contracted for the macadam for the road. For that reason I should like to have a definite statement regarding the project.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I will try, from recollection, to state the terms of the telegram that was sent to British Columbia and all the other provinces. It covered three phases of the situation and was accepted by all the provinces of Canada as a correct reflection of the conclusion arrived at on April 9 at the conference to which I have already alluded.

Unemployment-Agreements with Provinces
Worto that had been commenced, whereby loss would be occasioned if they were not completed, such as buildings, sewers and so forth, would be completed. Secondly, where undischarged contractual obligations existed- I used the term in its legal sense-that is to say, entire contracts, where the contractual obligation was apparent, it was obvious that the undertakings, no matter of what kind, would be completed. The message went on to say further that the provinces, the dominion contributing under arrangements to be made, would endeavour to take care of the situation in its entirety if possible by direct relief. Perhaps, in fact it is likely, I have not exactly quoted the telegram which was placed on Hansard when the resolution was introduced some weeks ago, but in substance I have given it correctly. If the situation in the municipality to which the hon. member refers is as he has stated it, the work will certainly have to be completed.

I noticed what the minister said about the desirability of the legislation being passed with as little delay as possible, and what the hon. member for Algoma said with respect to people suffering at the present time, and the inability to have their needs supplied until this federal legislation was passed. I think it is only proper in the circumstances to point out that the government must take the responsibility for leaving until the end of the session a measure that should have been brought in at the beginning. This is the most important legislation that has been before us, and it is rather unfortunate that it should have been left until the concluding weeks of the session before being introduced. I do not think the discussion has been unduly protracted, considering the importance of the legislation; certainly on this measure, it has not been.
The purpose I had in view before the minister spoke was not, however, to direct his attention to that phase of the question but rather-it may surprise him to learn this- to approve of one feature of the legislation and to make a suggestion in reference to it. This section provides for special relief works and undertakings in the national parks of Canada. I think that is a very desirable form of relief where relief has to be given. The government has property in the nature of great national parks, and if in these difficult times the unemployed could be put to work in those parks I can think of no particular form of relief which could be more acceptable to them and which at the same time would serve the interests of the government and of the country so well. Where there
can be work rather than simply relief or doles, I am sure it is better for the recipient of such assistance, and also for the state, which has to foot the bill.
May I, in that connection, ask the minister whether, when the government is considering its program under this provision, it mighl not extend the conception of "national parks' to government properties in this capital citj of Canada: in other words, whether some of the relief moneys might not be used by the Federal District Commission for the improving of some of the government properties in the Canadian capital. I know that already some steps have been taken in that direction. I am sorry the Minister of Public Works is not in the house, because I should have liked to express appreciation of what I know he has started to do in that respect. There is, for example, the property on Wellington street, part of which was burned down a fortnight or so ago. The part that remains constitutes a fire trap. It is government property, having been in the possession of the Dominion for some twenty years, and this would be a good time to take these properties down and make a park area there until later on, when something in the nature of additional public buildings may be warranted by the circumstances of the time.
What I have in mind is this. The walk which we have around Parliament hill, the walk that runs around the hill from Elgin street to Bank street, is, I believe, the result of work which was provided one year for the unemployed by the Mackenzie administration during the hard times from 1874 to 1878, and it has been of service to the country ever since. During the present hard times, where the unemployed are put to work with public money, if we can at the same time improve the appearance of the capital, particularly in so far as the government's own properties are concerned, the money will be well spent and will serve other purposes than merely providing unemployment relief.
In that connection may I say that if the government would continue to set an example to the city, the city might, with the aid of the Federal District Commission, clean up a good many of its properties. Some of them, as they stand at the present time, are eyesores in the capital; and this year, when everyone is making an effort to have the capital of the Dominion appear as presentable as possible, I should think that, whatever numbers of unemployed there are here who may be entitled to relief, might and would be glad to be put to work under the direction of the improvement commission, along with
